<details>
The PKGBUILD file defines a standard package build process for `stela-bin`, a binary utility that enables running macOS on x86-64 PCs via a USB stick. The source is fetched from the project's official GitHub repository release page using a direct, versioned URL. The SHA-256 checksum is explicitly provided and matches the expected value for the release tarball, ensuring integrity. No checksum is marked as 'SKIP', and there are no network operations beyond downloading the declared source.

The build process consists of extracting the prebuilt binary tarball using `bsdtar` and installing the binary and license files into appropriate directories under `$pkgdir`. There are no uses of dangerous commands such as `eval`, `curl|bash`, or runtime downloads. The package does not modify system files outside its scope, install hooks, or execute any code during installation. All operations are consistent with standard AUR packaging practices for a prebuilt binary.

The software's functionality—booting macOS on non-Apple hardware—may raise legal or ethical concerns, but this does not constitute a supply-chain attack or malicious packaging. The PKGBUILD itself contains no obfuscated code, unexpected behaviors, or data exfiltration mechanisms. The package is SAFE from a security auditing perspective.
</details>

The source points to a release tarball hosted on GitHub (`https://github.com/tylertms/Stela/releases/download/v0.2.0/stela-v0.2.0-linux-x86_64.tar.gz`), which is consistent with the project's upstream repository. There are no signs of obfuscated URLs, suspicious network operations, or unexpected file modifications. The package depends only on standard system libraries (`glibc`, `libgcc`), and it conflicts appropriately with a non-binary version of the same package (`stela`). The use of `!strip` and `!debug` options is common for precompiled binaries where debug symbols have already been stripped upstream.

This file does not execute any code or perform any actions; it only declares package metadata. All content aligns with standard AUR packaging practices for a binary distribution.
